content: To effectively manage insecticide resistance in malaria vectors, it is essential to monitor the distribution and use of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) post-deployment. This includes assessing coverage in terms of access and utilization. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends conducting studies on the durability and integrity of ITNs, particularly when new products, such as pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs, are introduced. These studies provide critical data on the lifespan of ITNs under field conditions and help estimate the duration of their additional impact against malaria. A systematic review revealed that two years after deployment, 39% of pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs were torn (defined as having a total hole area ≥ 790 cm²), compared to 28% of pyrethroid-only long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) and 43% of pyrethroid-PBO ITNs. Pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs can be deployed in areas with pyrethroid resistance as an alternative to pyrethroid-only LLINs for malaria prevention in adults and children. However, the recommendation to use pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs is conditional due to concerns about their cost-effectiveness compared to pyrethroid-only LLINs. The higher cost of pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs, combined with their relatively short-lived additional impact (approximately 12 months), makes them less economically viable. The WHO advises that ITNs prequalified by the organization should be selected for deployment. The recommendation to deploy pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs instead of pyrethroid-only LLINs is based on moderate certainty evidence. However, when compared to pyrethroid-PBO ITNs, pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs are not recommended due to their lower cost-effectiveness and limited evidence of superior impact. The evidence supporting this recommendation is derived from a single trial conducted in Africa. Pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs combine a pyrethroid insecticide, which rapidly kills mosquitoes by targeting their nervous system, with pyriproxyfen, an insect growth regulator (IGR) that disrupts mosquito reproduction and growth. While the pyrethroid component kills mosquitoes, the IGR sterilizes or reduces the fecundity of those that survive, thereby limiting the spread of insecticide-resistant mosquitoes. Pyriproxyfen also has some impact on mosquito lifespan. This dual-action mechanism makes pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs potentially more effective in areas with pyrethroid-resistant malaria vectors. The systematic review included three trials from Africa, which evaluated the impact of pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs on malaria incidence and infection prevalence compared to pyrethroid-only LLINs and pyrethroid-PBO ITNs. In areas of high malaria transmission and pyrethroid-resistant mosquitoes, clinical malaria incidence decreased by approximately 20% one year after deploying pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs and by 15% two years post-deployment. Malaria infection prevalence was reduced by 30% one year post-deployment and by 20% two years post-deployment. However, compared to pyrethroid-PBO ITNs, pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs were associated with a two-fold higher incidence of clinical malaria one year after deployment, with no significant effect on malaria infection prevalence. The cost-effectiveness of pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs is a significant concern. A trial in Tanzania reported that pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs incurred higher costs and averted fewer disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) compared to pyrethroid-PBO ITNs. The incremental cost of pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs was estimated at $9,621 per 10,000 population, while pyrethroid-PBO ITNs cost $4,816 per 10,000 population. Given flatlined funding for malaria programs, the higher cost of pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs could reduce ITN coverage and negatively impact equity, particularly in resource-constrained settings. The WHO panel concluded that while pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs may have a moderate impact against malaria compared to pyrethroid-only LLINs, their benefits are minor when compared to pyrethroid-PBO ITNs. The panel conditionally recommended against deploying pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs instead of pyrethroid-PBO ITNs in areas with insecticide resistance. This decision was based on the lack of evidence showing a greater impact of pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs and their lower cost-effectiveness. Without additional resources, switching to pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs could reduce coverage and equity, thereby undermining malaria control efforts.
